newsitem.title: USA: Albright says Arafat, Netanyahu recommit to peace.
newsitem.headline: Albright says Arafat, Netanyahu recommit to peace.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright said on Wednesday that Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat recommitted himself to ensuring Israel's security after a bombing in a crowded Jerusalem market.
She called Arafat from her airborne U.S. Air Force jet and was told "he was committed to restoring a secure atmosphere."

Speaking to reporters travelling with her from Asia, Albright said Arafat "said to me he condemned the act and that he was meeting with his security officials and that they were doing everything they could to make sure the security situation is restored."
"We must not allow terror to succeed in its aim of killing our hope and our search for peace," she added.

"But at the moment, the focus of all those committed to peace must be squarely on security -- on bringing to justice those responsible for this act and on comprehensive and effective steps to combat terror," she added.

Hours earlier, two Arab suicide bombers killed 15 people and wounded more than 150 in a crowded Jerusalem market on Wednesday, setting back fresh U.S. efforts to resolve an Israel-PLO peace crisis that has now deepened.
It was the deadliest attack against Israelis since March 1996.

Israeli police said the bombers, wearing jackets and ties, strolled into crowds of lunchtime shoppers at the Mahane Yehuda market in west Jerusalem with 22-pound bombs concealed in attache cases and blew themselves up.
U.S. officials said they understoood that the bombers may have been dressed up as orthodox Jews. "Everyone assumes they were Palestinians dressed up in disguises," one official said.
The Islamic militant movement Hamas claimed responsibility for the attack in a leaflet faxed to an international news agency.
From the airplane, Albright also spoke with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

"We talked about the importance of returning to the peace process and I urged him to do so and he said he understood the importance of returning to the peace process," she said. "He did say he would (return to the process."
Albright was expected to speak again to both leaders once she was on the ground in Honolulu.

She had planned to stay overnight after a week-long trip to Malaysia and Singapore but cut short the stay because of the bombing. She will be in Hawaii about 15 hours -- the period of time that Air Force regulations require for the pilots to rest between flights.

On returning to Washington on Thursday, she planned to reassess with President Bill Clinton when to reschedule a trip to the region by U.S. Middle East coordinator Dennis Ross that was delayed to allow a period of mourning in the Jewish state.
He had been set to depart on Thursday or Friday with the aim of presenting to Israelis and Palestinians new ideas on ending a deadlock to peace negotiations, due to Israeli settlement-building.
"One of the things we have to figure out is what is the most appropriate time for us to renew and have him go back," she said.
Albright bridled at suggestions that because she has not visited the Middle East since taking office six months ago, she has not been sufficiently involved in peacemaking there.

"I am directly involved. Let us make this clear. I have been since the day I became secretary of state," meeting with Middle East leaders on visits to Washington and talking to them on the telephone, she said.
"You do not have to be in the region to be personally involved," she said.
